subject: Quantitative Aptitude
topic: Profit and loss III — mixed tiers
description: Successive discounts, marked price, multi-step P&L, equivalent discount, dishonest dealer

questions.stem: An article is bought for ₹400 and sold for ₹460. The profit percent is:
questions.explanation: Profit = SP − CP = 460 − 400 = 60. Profit% = 60/400 × 100 = 15%. Distractor 10% comes from 60/600. Distractor 12% from 60/500. Distractor 20% from 60/300.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.topic: Profit and loss III — mixed tiers

questions.stem: Two successive discounts of 20% and 10% on a marked price of ₹500 give a final selling price of:
questions.explanation: After 20% discount: 500 × 0.8 = 400. After further 10% discount: 400 × 0.9 = 360. Equivalent single discount = 1 − (0.8)(0.9) = 1 − 0.72 = 28%. Distractor 350 comes from a flat 30% discount (wrong, since successive ≠ added). Distractor 400 stops at the first discount. Distractor 340 from a 32% flat (over-counts).
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.topic: Profit and loss III — mixed tiers

questions.stem: A shopkeeper marks his goods 25% above cost price and offers a 10% discount on the marked price. His net profit percent is:
questions.explanation: Let CP = 100. MP = 125. SP after 10% discount = 125 × 0.9 = 112.5. Profit = 12.5. Profit% = 12.5/100 × 100 = 12.5%. Distractor 10% confuses with the discount rate. Distractor 15% is mark-up minus discount (wrong because successive ≠ subtractive). Distractor 25% confuses with mark-up rate.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.topic: Profit and loss III — mixed tiers

questions.stem: A man sells two articles at ₹600 each. On one he gains 20% and on the other he loses 20%. His overall result on the deal is:

options.option_text: Neither gain nor loss
Loss of 4% overall
Gain of 4% overall
Loss of 2% overall

questions.explanation: When same SP gives equal % gain on one and equal % loss on other, there is ALWAYS a NET LOSS of (x²/100)% where x is the common percentage. Here x = 20 → loss = 400/100 = 4%. Verify: CP1 = 600/1.2 = 500; CP2 = 600/0.8 = 750; total CP = 1250; total SP = 1200 → loss = 50, % = 50/1250 = 4%. Distractor 1 is the common-sense WRONG answer (intuition says they cancel). Distractor 3 has the right magnitude but wrong sign. Distractor 4 has the right sign but wrong magnitude.
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.topic: Profit and loss III — mixed tiers

questions.stem: A dishonest dealer claims to sell at cost price but uses a 900-gram weight in place of 1 kg. His actual profit percent is:
questions.explanation: Customer pays for 1000 g but receives 900 g. Profit% = (true wt − false wt) / false wt × 100 = (1000 − 900) / 900 × 100 = 100/9 ≈ 11.11%. Distractor 10% uses wrong denominator (1000). Distractor 9% has digits flipped. Distractor 12.5% from 100/8 (used 800 g — common slip).
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.topic: Profit and loss III — mixed tiers

questions.stem: If the marked price of a watch is ₹1200 and a single discount of 25% is offered, the selling price is:
questions.explanation: Discount = 25% of 1200 = 300. SP = 1200 − 300 = 900. Equivalently SP = 1200 × 0.75 = 900. Distractor 950 from 1200 − 250 (used 250 instead of 300). Distractor 1000 from 1200 − 200 (used 200). Distractor 1175 from 1200 − 25 (treated 25 as flat ₹).
questions.subject: Quantitative Aptitude
questions.topic: Profit and loss III — mixed tiers

questions.stem: A person sells a chair for ₹720 with a profit of 20%. To gain 25% on the same chair, the new selling price would be:
questions.explanation: CP = SP / (1 + profit%) = 720 / 1.20 = 600. New SP for 25% profit = 600 × 1.25 = 750. Distractor 740 from 720 + 20 (added rough premium). Distractor 780 from 720 × 25/24 (mis-ratio). Distractor 800 from 720 × 1.11 (used wrong factor).

questions.topic: Profit and loss III — mixed tiers

questions.stem: A merchant earns a profit that is exactly 20% of the selling price of an article. What is his profit expressed as a percentage of the cost price?

options.option_text: 25% — for every ₹80 of cost, ₹20 profit is earned
20% — same percentage holds for both CP and SP bases
22.5% — midpoint between SP-based and CP-based rates
16.67% — obtained by inverting the SP-based rate

questions.explanation: Profit = 20% of SP means CP = 80% of SP. So Profit/CP = (0.2 × SP)/(0.8 × SP) = 25%. Option B (20%) is wrong — it merely restates the SP-based rate without converting the denominator from SP to CP.

questions.stem: A fruit vendor buys apples at 5 for ₹20 and sells them at 4 for ₹20. What is his profit percentage on the cost price?

options.option_text: 25% — SP per apple is ₹5 against CP of ₹4 each
20% — profit measured against selling price of ₹5
15% — taking arithmetic difference of the batch rates
33.33% — using unsold apple as fraction of sold lot

questions.explanation: CP per apple = ₹20 ÷ 5 = ₹4; SP per apple = ₹20 ÷ 4 = ₹5. Profit% = (5 − 4)/4 × 100 = 25%. Option B (20%) is wrong — it computes profit on SP (1/5 = 20%) instead of on CP, a classic base-confusion error.

questions.stem: A grain merchant blends Type-A rice (bought at ₹40/kg) and Type-B rice (bought at ₹60/kg) in the ratio 3 : 2 by weight, then sells the blend at ₹57/kg. What is his profit percentage?

options.option_text: 14% — using simple unweighted average of both rates
18.75% — weighted CP of ₹48 versus selling rate ₹57
9.6% — ratio reversed to 2 : 3 by computational error
15.79% — profit calculated as share of selling price

questions.explanation: Weighted CP = (3 × 40 + 2 × 60)/5 = (120 + 120)/5 = ₹48/kg. Profit% = (57 − 48)/48 × 100 = 18.75%. Option A (14%) is wrong — it uses the unweighted average CP of ₹50 instead of the 3 : 2 weighted cost of ₹48.

questions.stem: A trader marks an article 30% above cost price and then offers a discount on the marked price so that he still earns exactly a 4% profit on cost. What discount percentage did he offer?

options.option_text: 30% — applying the full markup rate as the discount
20% — ₹26 off marked price of ₹130 gives 20% off
26% — discount of ₹26 divided by cost price of ₹100
4% — equating the discount to the stated profit margin

questions.explanation: Let CP = 100, so MP = 130 and required SP = 104. Discount% = (130 − 104)/130 × 100 = 26/130 × 100 = 20%. Option C (26%) is the most common error — candidates divide the rupee discount (₹26) by CP (₹100) instead of MP (₹130).

questions.stem: A garment store offers successive discounts of 20% and 10% on a saree marked at ₹1,500. A rival store offers a flat 25% discount on the same saree. Which deal is better for the buyer, and by how much?

options.option_text: Rival store's deal, saving ₹25 on the listed price
First store's deal, cheaper by ₹45 for the buyer
Both deals give the same final price of ₹1,125
Rival store's deal, as 25% exceeds any two-step rate

questions.explanation: First store: 1500 × 0.80 × 0.90 = ₹1,080. Rival store: 1500 × 0.75 = ₹1,125. First store is cheaper by ₹45. Option D is wrong — successive 20% + 10% gives an effective 28% discount (not 20%), which beats the rival's flat 25%.

questions.stem: A manufacturer sells goods to a wholesaler at 20% profit; the wholesaler sells to a retailer at 25% profit; the retailer sells to a customer at 20% profit for ₹1,800. What is the manufacturer's cost price?

options.option_text: ₹1,000 — correct three-stage reverse price calculation
₹1,200 — only two of the three profit stages reversed
₹1,091 — additive 65% markup applied as single divisor
₹1,440 — subtracting 20% from final price erroneously

questions.explanation: Retailer CP = 1800 ÷ 1.20 = ₹1,500; Wholesaler CP = 1500 ÷ 1.25 = ₹1,200; Manufacturer CP = 1200 ÷ 1.20 = ₹1,000. Option B (₹1,200) is wrong — it skips the manufacturer's own 20% profit stage, stopping one step too early in the reverse chain.

questions.stem: A stationery wholesaler buys 500 pens at ₹40 each and marks each pen at ₹60. He sells 300 pens at a 10% discount on the marked price and the remaining 200 pens at a 20% discount. What is his net profit percentage on total cost?

options.option_text: 29% profit — discounts applied correctly on marked price
14% loss — discounts mistakenly applied on cost price
22.5% profit — profit divided by revenue, not by cost
50% profit — using only the MP-to-CP markup ratio

questions.explanation: Total CP = 500 × 40 = ₹20,000. Revenue: 300 × 60 × 0.90 = ₹16,200 plus 200 × 60 × 0.80 = ₹9,600 = ₹25,800 total. Profit% = (25,800 − 20,000)/20,000 × 100 = 29%. Option B (14% loss) is wrong — it applies the discounts to CP (₹40) instead of the marked price (₹60), which inverts the profit into a loss.
